correctness.rationale: For each prime \(p\), the proof identifies membership by the exact integer count \(D_p(N)=\lfloor N/p\rfloor-\lfloor N/(p+1)\rfloor\) and proves the exact increment identity \(D_p(N)-D_p(N-1)=\mathbf 1_{p\mid N}-\mathbf 1_{p+1\mid N}\). Primes below the square-root boundary occur at both steps; at or above the boundary the interval contains at most one integer. Oddness of \(N\ge5\) eliminates every loss term because \(p+1\) is even. At most one prime divisor can meet the square-root boundary. The square case and the exceptional \(N=3\) are handled explicitly. A separate finite checker through \(100000\) agrees with the theorem but is not used as proof.

originality.rationale: Heyman explicitly states the three-prime dichotomy as Conjecture 4 after proving only the prime and two-prime cases. The later Ma--Wu paper strengthens asymptotic estimates but does not state an exact one-step criterion. Current MathDB still marks the conjecture open, and OEIS A067514 has no largest-prime-factor step formula. Targeted semantic searches for the conjecture, the odd-step law, and the largest-prime-factor formulation returned no covering result. The new theorem strictly broadens the conjecture from one three-prime shape to every odd integer \(N\ge5\).
residual_risks: An obscure unpublished, non-indexed, or differently phrased proof could exist.

value.rationale: The result resolves a named conjecture from the focal literature and replaces its three-prime case split with a structural theorem valid for every odd integer \(N\ge5\). The proof identifies the exact mechanism of changes in the prime floor set: only a prime factor at the square-root boundary can enter at an odd step, and no large prime can leave. This is a natural strengthening rather than an arbitrary finite slice.
